lead: A rolling bearing fails by fatigue, not at one fixed load. Heavy load shortens life. Makers give two numbers: C, the basic dynamic load rating, and C0, the basic static load rating. From C and equivalent load P you get L10, the life reached by 90 of 100 bearings. This chapter computes L10 = (C/P)^p in million revolutions, then in hours.
prereq: Need Chapter 5.2 for bearing parts and Unit 2 for fatigue.

blocks.text: A ball or roller bearing rarely snaps. It fails by fatigue: after many revolutions a small piece of raceway metal flakes off, called spalling. Life depends on load. Roughly, double the load and a ball bearing lasts one-eighth as long. Standards give two ratings.

items: Basic static load rating C0, in N: the load that leaves a permanent dent of 0.0001 times the ball diameter at the most heavily loaded contact. Use C0 for stationary, slow, or heavy shock at rest.
Basic dynamic load rating C, in N: the load at which identical bearings reach a rating life of one million (10⁶) revolutions with 90% healthy. C is capacity, not breaking load.

blocks.text: Both come from the catalogue, not from derivation. For a 25 mm bore deep-groove ball bearing, C is about 14 kN and C0 about 8 kN. Use them to form the ratio C/P.
A real bearing carries radial load F<sub>r</sub>, in N, perpendicular to the shaft axis, and axial or thrust load F<sub>a</sub>, in N, along the axis. Fold both into one equivalent dynamic load P.

blocks.where: P in N; F<sub>r</sub> radial load in N; F<sub>a</sub> axial load in N; X radial factor, Y thrust factor, from the catalogue for that bearing.

blocks.text: P is the pure radial load giving the same fatigue as the actual mix. For pure radial load, X = 1, Y = 0, so P = F<sub>r</sub>. For pure thrust load, X = 0, so P = Y F<sub>a</sub>.

Single-row deep-groove ball bearings take small thrust. Catalogue tables compare F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> with threshold e and F<sub>a</sub>/C0. If F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> ≤ e, X = 1, Y = 0, so P = F<sub>r</sub>. Above e, X = 0.56 and Y comes from the table, typically 1 to 2. Use tables for the chosen bearing type.

sections.h3: Life in revolutions and in hours

blocks.where: L<sub>10</sub> is rating life in million revolutions; C and P are in the same unit (N or kN); p = 3 for ball bearings, p = 10/3 for roller bearings.

blocks.text: The subscript 10 is a probability, not a count. L<sub>10</sub> is the life 90% of a batch reaches; about 10% fail earlier. C = 30 kN, P = 6 kN gives L<sub>10</sub> = (30/6)³ = 125 million revolutions. The same C on a roller bearing gives 5<sup>10/3</sup> ≈ 214 million, because a roller spreads contact over a line.

blocks.where: L<sub>10h</sub> is life in hours; n is speed in rpm; 10⁶ converts million revolutions to revolutions; 60 converts minutes to hours.

blocks.text: At n = 1500 rpm: L<sub>10h</sub> = 10⁶ × 125/(60 × 1500) = 1389 hours, about 58 days of continuous running. At half speed the hours double.

For stepped load and speed, use P<sub>e</sub> = [ (P<sub>1</sub><sup>p</sup> n<sub>1</sub> t<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub><sup>p</sup> n<sub>2</sub> t<sub>2</sub> + …)/(n<sub>1</sub> t<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub> t<sub>2</sub> + …) ]<sup>1/p</sup>, where t<sub>i</sub> is time in each step. For reliability other than 90%, multiply L<sub>10</sub> by a<sub>1</sub>: about 0.62 for 95%, 0.21 for 99%.

figure.caption: Life falls steeply as load rises: at 6 kN the curve gives 125 million revolutions, the marked worked-example point; at 10 kN it is 27 million.

spec.aria: The curve falls steeply; at 6 kN equivalent load the life is 125 million revolutions.

examples.question: A deep-groove ball bearing on a pump shaft has C = 30 kN. The shaft runs at n = 1500 rpm. The equivalent dynamic load is P = 6 kN. Find L10 in million revolutions and in hours.
steps: Check units: C = 30 kN and P = 6 kN are both kN, so C/P is dimensionless.
examples.answer: L10 = 125 million revolutions, which at 1500 rpm is L10h ≈ 1389 hours.
examples.check:
C = 30.0    # kN, basic dynamic load rating
P = 6.0     # kN, equivalent dynamic load
n = 1500.0  # rpm
L10 = (C / P) ** 3          # million revolutions
L10h = 1e6 * L10 / (60 * n) # hours
print(round(L10, 1))
print(round(L10h, 0))

traps: Mixing newtons and kilonewtons inside C/P. Convert C and P to the same unit before dividing.
Using p = 3 for a roller bearing. Rollers take p = 10/3, and the same C/P then gives a longer life.
Putting F<sub>r</sub> in place of P when the bearing also carries thrust. If F<sub>a</sub>/F<sub>r</sub> > e, P > F<sub>r</sub> and life drops.
Dropping the 10⁶ when converting L<sub>10</sub> to L<sub>10h</sub>; the answer becomes a million times too small.
Reading L<sub>10</sub> as the life every bearing reaches or as 10% reliability. It is the 90% reliability life.
Using C0 in the life formula. C0 guards against permanent denting at rest; only C enters L<sub>10</sub>.

quiz.q: Define the basic dynamic load rating C of a rolling bearing.
quiz.a: C, in N, is the load at which identical bearings reach one million revolutions with 90% still serviceable.

quiz.q: What does the subscript 10 in L10 stand for?
quiz.a: 10% of bearings fail before L10; 90% reach it. L10 is a 90% reliability life.

quiz.q: Why does L10 fall sharply when P rises slightly?
quiz.a: L10 varies as (C/P)^p with p = 3 or more. A 20% rise in P cuts life to about 1/1.2³, roughly 58% of its old value.

quiz.q: Write the equivalent dynamic load formula and say what X and Y are, and when P equals Fr.
quiz.a: P = X Fr + Y Fa; Fr is radial load in N, Fa axial load in N, X radial factor, Y thrust factor, from the catalogue. When Fa/Fr ≤ e, X = 1, Y = 0, so P = Fr.

quiz.q: A deep-groove ball bearing has C = 24 kN and carries P = 4 kN at n = 1000 rpm. Find L10 in million revolutions and L10h in hours.
quiz.a: C/P = 24/4 = 6; p = 3, so L10 = 6³ = 216 million revolutions. L10h = 10⁶ × 216/(60 × 1000) = 3600 hours.

quiz.q: A spherical roller bearing has C = 60 kN and carries P = 12 kN at n = 500 rpm. Find L10h in hours.
quiz.a: C/P = 5. For a roller bearing p = 10/3, so L10 = 5^(10/3) ≈ 214 million revolutions. L10h = 10⁶ × 214/(60 × 500) ≈ 7130 hours.

quiz.q: A bearing with C = 30 kN carries P = 6 kN at 1500 rpm, giving L10 = 125 million revolutions and 1389 hours. The load doubles to P = 12 kN at the same speed. Find the new life and state what this says about overloading.
quiz.a: New C/P = 30/12 = 2.5, so L10 = 2.5³ = 15.625 million revolutions. L10h = 10⁶ × 15.625/90 000 ≈ 174 hours. Life falls to one-eighth; a modest overload can ruin the bearing within days.

quiz.q: In L10h = (10⁶/(60 n))(C/P)^p, why does a bearing last longer in hours at lower speed even though its life in revolutions is unchanged?
quiz.a: Life in revolutions depends only on C/P, not speed. At lower speed those revolutions take more hours; the factor 60n in the denominator makes hours rise as n falls.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plain L10 assumes clean lubricant, normal clearance and good alignment. Life-modification methods multiply it by factors for lubrication, contamination and steel fatigue limit, so catalogues quote longer lives. Condition monitoring uses vibration and temperature to estimate used L10 life and replace a bearing before failure. Search ISO 281, life modification factor and vibration signature analysis.
